title: A Model for Projected Water Needs and Intervention Strategies in India

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF page 1 is the summary sheet, PDF page 2 is the contents/title page, and PDF pages 3-23 are internally numbered pages 2-22.

context_sources.use: Official COMAP page 1 supports only the high-level theme and report expectations; page 2 confirms control 43443 as an Outstanding Winner; pages 2-5 are award tables. The document is not the complete official statement.

limitations: All 23 paper pages were rendered and reviewed through four contact sheets; core formulas on PDF pages 6, 10-13 and forecast figures on pages 14 and 20 were inspected at full resolution.
The complete official 2016 Problem E statement is absent from the corpus; only a COMAP press-release summary and result designation are authoritative context.
Text extraction is strong, but several apostrophes and bullet glyphs are mojibake; equation meaning was taken from rendered pages.
No source data table, MATLAB code, fit degree, polynomial coefficients, random or numerical settings, machine-readable figure series, or complete uncertainty derivation is supplied.
The printed complex-model EWR equation reverses the sign of the original definition, creating a source-level formula inconsistency rather than an extraction ambiguity.
Long-horizon zero-crossing claims extend decades beyond the displayed 2000-2050 figures and the last stated 2050 government projection knot.

official_supported_requirements: Understand the drivers of water scarcity.
Create intervention strategies for a region to mitigate a water crisis.
Use thorough data analysis, creative modeling, scientific methodology, effective writing, and visualization.
Communicate the work in a 20-page report.
unknown_official_clauses: The complete wording, region-selection conditions, forecast horizon, required questions, stakeholder requirements, surrounding-region requirement, and deliverable details are not present in reviewed authoritative context.
Paper section titles and implied subquestions cannot be labeled official.
paper_implied_tasks: Choose a region and identify physical and social drivers.
Forecast the region's water status over roughly 15 years and farther into the future.
Design interventions and analyze effects on the selected and surrounding areas.
Evaluate strengths and weaknesses and recommend a policy direction.
task_reconstruction.paper_approach: Define an Excess Water Ratio as renewable surplus per capita, compare it algebraically with WSI, choose India, diagnose agricultural and access drivers, build an exponential sector-growth stress model and a MATLAB polynomial interpolation model from Indian government scenarios, evaluate watershed development, wastewater reuse, dietary change, and millet substitution, and compare long-run zero-crossing dates.
task_reconstruction.coverage_gap: The paper covers the supported high-level official themes, but full official coverage is unprovable. Core balance, unit, arithmetic, model-reconciliation, validation, uncertainty, cost, feasibility, spatial, quality, and distributional gaps prevent the recommendations from being treated as operational.

section_map.summary: Introduces EWR, India, two forecast models, supply- and demand-side interventions, a half-by-2031 claim, and distant zero-crossing dates.
Lists indicator construction, evaluation, India drivers, forecasts, interventions, surrounding effects, projections, and conclusion.
Motivates water scarcity through biological needs, global use shares, accessible freshwater limits, population growth, pollution, and food demand.
Defines WSI and motivates per-capita unused renewable water as a new scarcity indicator.
States runoff-only supply, monotonic utility, temporary equilibrium, perfect safety knowledge, and no spatial-distribution assumptions, then defines the basic EWR.
Relates agricultural, industrial, personal, and runoff components to production, footprints, population, climate, and technology.
Compares WSI and EWR for ten countries and argues population makes individual impact clearer.
Claims population and predictive advantages, notes data and aggregation limits, and adds environmental water and imports.
Selects India and identifies rainfall variability, irrigation feedback, groundwater depletion, agriculture, population, and contamination.
Inverts WSI to estimate 20.75 m3 or 5481.59 gallons of renewable surplus per person per year.
Defines industrial, agricultural, and domestic demand from production, footprints, urban-rural populations, and growth rates.
Projects 1.306 trillion m3 of use and negative EWR before 2031, then introduces polynomial fits to government projection knots.
Lists seven use categories, prints a sign-reversed EWR equation, and adds illustrative 30 and 50 billion m3 intervention shocks.
Plots upper and lower EWR paths with and without example interventions from 2000 to 2050.
Assumes government scenarios and polynomial approximation are accurate, then discusses urbanization, constrained growth, health, and sanitation.
Frames supply versus demand, rejects dams on social and ecological grounds, and sizes 50 watershed projects with a factor-of-ten arithmetic error.
Scales wastewater treatment, discusses diet, and proposes more water-efficient crop production.
Models full rice-and-wheat substitution by millet and records wastewater salinity, waterlogging, and downstream health risks.
Discusses watershed economics and gender effects, reuse costs and jobs, and millet taste, training, seed, and finance barriers.
Compares infrastructure and millet scenario curves through 2050 while the prose extrapolates zero crossings beyond 2080.
Favors demand reduction over infrastructure and concludes much larger societal change is required, without reconciling model conflicts.
Lists water, population, climate, scarcity-index, India, and source-data references.
Lists government, intervention, watershed, wastewater, crop, and adoption sources.

contributions.summary: Turns renewable surplus into an intuitive per-capita physical unit rather than leaving scarcity as a dimensionless withdrawal ratio.
Separates agriculture, industry, households, population, footprints, output, climate, and runoff into a forecastable dependency structure.
Recognizes environmental water requirements and imported water that the initial WSI-like balance omits.
Combines hydrologic variability, infrastructure finance, groundwater depletion, agricultural dominance, growth, and contamination.
Uses a transparent stress calculation alongside an official-scenario interpolation, exposing sensitivity to model structure even though it does not reconcile the results.
Considers watershed development, wastewater reuse, diet, crop production, and dam counterexamples across supply and demand.
Explicitly records downstream salinity, waterlogging, groundwater quality, and health risks from reuse.
Reports that watershed projects can harm poorer women through loss of common grazing land and calls for participation.
Connects millet feasibility to consumer taste, local demand, farmer training, seed finance, and smallholder support.
Distinguishes limited supply-side increments from potentially larger demand-side change and conditions success on implementation.

broken_or_weak_links: The complex EWR equation reverses the original sign.
The plotted forecast scale is not reconciled with the reported 2009 EWR baseline.
The stress and polynomial forecasts give incompatible shortage timing.
Watershed benefit arithmetic is wrong by a factor of ten.
Costs, adoption, uncertainty, and externalities are not integrated into policy rankings.
No independent forecast or intervention validation supports the final recommendation.

assumptions.summary: Treats mean annual runoff as the only water source in the first model.
Assumes every increase in available water benefits every individual regardless of use, quality, or baseline.
Assumes aggregate use cannot exceed available water and omits stock depletion and transfers.
Assumes people and government know source safety and allocate water appropriately.
Ignores transport, basin, seasonal, and within-country distribution of water and demand.
Assumes individual personal use remains constant except under large economic change.
Holds mean annual runoff constant over 15 years despite expected climate effects.
Sets agricultural and industrial footprint growth to zero and compounds sector output growth.
Treats government projections as accurate and polynomial functions as adequate between sparse knots.
Assumes all rice and wheat can transition to millet over 30 years for the modeled policy effect.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Uses WSI, withdrawals, runoff, and population for ten countries without a machine-readable table of source years and transformations beyond displayed values.
Uses AQUASTAT and secondary sources for rainfall, irrigation, groundwater, agriculture, population, and contamination.
Combines 2009 WSI, withdrawals, and a population value from cited sources to reconstruct national EWR.
Uses World Bank urban-rural population growth, average urban use, sector growth, and sector withdrawals.
Uses Indian government projected categories for 1997, 2010, 2025, and 2050 as sparse polyfit inputs.
Uses a meta-analysis, project hectares, cultivated area, and national irrigation withdrawals, but mixes cultivated area and water use with a factor-of-ten arithmetic error.
Uses counts, capacity, treated volume, and untreated volume to scale a national treatment buildout.
Uses crop water-depth values and nutrition assertions without a national crop-area, effective-rainfall, yield, price, or adoption dataset.
Cites 42 sources but does not publish aligned source data, versions, fit inputs, coefficients, code, or output series.

models.summary: Uses withdrawals divided by mean annual runoff as the baseline scarcity ratio.
Defines renewable surplus after three withdrawal categories per person.
Adds imports and environmental water requirements to the balance.
Reconstructs mean annual runoff and EWR from a published WSI, withdrawal, and population.
Models agricultural and industrial use as output times footprint and domestic use from urban-rural population.
Compounds fixed sector growth and footprint assumptions for 15 years.
Fits government category projections with MATLAB polyfit and combines them into EWR.
Estimates added agricultural water from average irrigated withdrawal per cultivated hectare and hectares per project.
Divides untreated wastewater by average plant capacity to estimate 651 facilities and 11.03 billion m3 per year.
Estimates water savings from rice and wheat water-depth differences under full millet replacement.

verification.summary: Compares EWR with the algebraically related WSI across ten countries, a circular rather than independent validation.
The WSI inversion reproduces about 20.748 m3, 5481 gallons, or 15 gallons/day per person.
The compounded sector inputs reproduce approximately 1.306 trillion m3, but no hindcast or uncertainty is shown.
The printed complex EWR sign conflicts with the basic EWR and blocks invariant consistency.
Upper and lower curves are displayed without fit degree, coefficients, calibration, or a statistical interval definition.
Independent unit recalculation exposes a tenfold error in per-hectare, per-project, and 50-project water gains.
The reported 651 facilities approximately follows from aggregate capacity, but utilization and feasibility remain unvalidated.
Figures end in 2050 while claims extend beyond 2080 and no extrapolation diagnostics are supplied.
The stress, polynomial, and summary results disagree materially and are not compared on common units and baselines.
No executable or machine-readable artifacts permit regeneration of forecasts, crossings, or policy comparisons.

results_trace.summary: Reports 20.75 m3 or 5481.59 gallons per person per year from a reproducible WSI inversion, but interprets hydrologic balance too close to accessible surplus.
Predicts 1.306 trillion m3 of use and negative EWR before 2031 under fixed footprints and exponential sector growth.
Shows decreasing curves through 2050 with an undocumented scale and no reconciliation to the 2009 baseline.
Recommends 50 semi-arid projects beginning immediately, but the modeled gain is understated tenfold and feasibility is incomplete.
Estimates 651 plants and full use of 11.03 billion m3 untreated wastewater, without cost or rollout feasibility.
Models full wheat and rice substitution over 30 years and projects much larger savings than infrastructure.
Documents downstream health risks, women's livelihood loss, maintenance failures, costs, jobs, and crop-adoption barriers.
Reports 2083-2093 without intervention, 2084-2094 with infrastructure, and 2097-2107 with millet despite plots ending in 2050.
Concludes demand-side cultural change is more consequential than the modeled supply projects, conditional on implementation.

writing_logic.summary: Gives a complete metric-case-forecast-intervention-result arc and foregrounds exact years and policy contrast.
Starts from an established WSI, identifies a decision-relevant limitation, and proposes a per-capita extension.
Separates strengths and weaknesses before extending the model, a useful revision-oriented structure.
Moves from national urgency to specific physical, infrastructure, agricultural, demographic, and quality drivers.
Labels the first model simplistic and more extreme, but fails to resolve the resulting forecast disagreement.
Organizes policies into supply and demand and uses driver dominance to focus on agriculture.
Pairs physical benefit with downstream, gender, cost, maintenance, taste, training, and finance consequences.
Returns from individual projects to the strategic supply-versus-demand message, but suppresses unresolved model defects.

All 13 earlier functional sections map into 12 normalized language chapters: the distinct indicator-evaluation function is retained across robustness-verification and strengths-limitations, so no source section is omitted; priority remains language imitation, positive organization logic, model and visual retention, then formula warnings.

language_observations.summary: Uses concrete values and contrasts infrastructure with millet effectively, but presents unresolved scenario results as a unified conclusion.
Explains WSI, its limitation, and EWR in accessible physical terms before introducing equations.
Clear bullets improve scanability, but precision and predictive-power claims exceed evidence.
Calls the exponential model simplistic, more extreme, and worst-case, a useful qualifier that should also appear in the summary.
Uses sourced concrete mechanisms rather than generic statements when describing downstream harm.
Connects adoption to recognizable actors and constraints: consumers, farmers, training, seed finance, and government capacity.
Uses strong policy language despite sign, arithmetic, scale, forecast, and feasibility gaps not carried forward.

visualization_observations.summary: Pairs a ten-country table with a compact scatterplot, but the algebraic dependence and extreme scale reduce its validation value.
Uses shared axes and separate panels, but lacks units, observed data markers, fit knots, intervention markers, and bound definitions.
Four colored scenario curves reveal the intervention's small modeled effect through 2050.
A parallel chart makes the larger demand-side scenario visually comparable to infrastructure.
Neither chart displays the 2083-2107 zero-crossing horizon supporting the text.
The plotted 2000 level near 1200 is not reconciled with the stated 2009 baseline of 20.75 m3 or 5481.59 gallons per person.
Upper and lower labels imply uncertainty but no probabilistic, scenario, or calibration basis is explained.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: C: Starting from an established metric, making its limitation intuitive, and carrying a coherent case-study structure may have improved readability, but no judge rationale is available.

C: Combining hydrology, agriculture, economics, health, gender, infrastructure, and adoption may align with the official emphasis on interdisciplinary work, but cannot establish why the paper received Outstanding.

weaknesses.summary: WSI-derived renewable surplus does not measure groundwater stock, storage, return flow, quality, reliability, affordability, access, or distribution.
The first balance omits groundwater mining, reservoirs, imports, reuse, desalination, and environmental depletion.
The claim that use cannot exceed physically available water confuses renewable flow with stored stocks and transfers.
Perfect knowledge and appropriate use conflict with the documented contamination and waterborne-disease context.
Ignoring geography and transport contradicts India's spatial and temporal rainfall variability and local access failures.
EWR-WSI correlation is partly algebraic and does not validate household, ecological, or predictive outcomes.
Precision and predictive power are asserted without forecast errors, holdouts, uncertainty, or criterion outcomes.
Hydrologic balance is translated into extra individual water despite acknowledged inaccessibility and contamination.
Climate effects are acknowledged but omitted rather than represented as scenarios with correlated demand impacts.
Fixed footprints and exponential sector growth omit scarcity feedback, prices, efficiency, technology, and structural change.
Negative EWR is described as out of water instead of demand exceeding the modeled renewable balance.
Four government projection knots are fitted without degree, coefficients, residuals, physical constraints, or extrapolation tests.
The complex EWR equation reverses availability minus use to use minus availability.
30 and 50 billion m3 additions are demonstrations without project, cost, capacity, or evidence basis.
Graph units and the relationship to the 2009 baseline are undocumented.
2031 negative, half-by-2031, and 2083-2093 zero results are not reconciled.
Per-hectare and project water gains are understated by a factor of ten.
National cultivated area, irrigation withdrawal, constant hectare demand, project representativeness, capacity, cost, and maintenance are insufficiently aligned.
Full treatment and agricultural reuse assume 651 plants, three-year construction, and no collection, energy, quality, siting, or financing constraints.
A 100% rice-and-wheat substitution omits regional suitability, crop area, effective rainfall, yield, diet, trade, prices, adoption, and rebound.
Salinity, waterlogging, and downstream health harms are discussed but not subtracted from net water or welfare benefit.
Wastewater plants are called worthwhile despite unavailable prices and acknowledged fiscal infeasibility.
Zero-crossing intervals decades after 2050 are unsupported by displayed data and model diagnostics.
Upper and lower curves have no stated derivation, coverage meaning, or calibration.
No global parameter, structural, adoption, feasibility, decision-reversal, or value-of-information analysis is performed.
No aligned data, code, coefficients, exact figure values, or threshold calculations permit regeneration.

independent_extensions.summary: Rebuild EWR as a basin-season stock-flow and quality balance with groundwater, storage, return flows, imports, exports, ecological reserves, treatment, access, and uncertainty.

Pair renewable balance per capita with household access, reliability, affordability, health, ecological deficit, and subgroup distributions rather than claiming one indicator measures individual impact.
Validate the indicator against held-out basin shortages, service interruptions, prices, waterborne disease, groundwater decline, and ecological outcomes.
Replace unconstrained sparse polyfit extrapolation with physically bounded, monotone, scenario-aware models and show model-form divergence beyond 2050.
Reconcile the sector-growth and government-scenario forecasts on common baseline years, units, historical hindcasts, and explicit central versus stress labels.
Add automated unit, sign, mass-balance, arithmetic, baseline, and figure-series invariants before interpreting any policy output.
Recalculate watershed benefits using region-specific irrigated area, crop demand, effective rainfall, storage, project performance distributions, limits, costs, maintenance, and gender effects.
Design wastewater reuse as a staged network portfolio with collection, plant capacity, utilization, energy, quality, salinity, siting, delivery, finance, operations, and downstream protection.
Model partial crop substitution by region and season with yields, irrigation, nutrition, taste, prices, trade, training, seed finance, farmer welfare, and rebound.
Use robust multiobjective portfolio optimization over water, cost, health, ecology, equity, food security, and feasibility instead of comparing technical volumes alone.
Run global sensitivity, structural alternatives, scenario reoptimization, shortage-date distributions, ranking reversals, and value-of-information analysis.
Publish aligned source tables, transformations, coefficients, code, environment, exact result tables, figure data, and one-command reproduction.

candidate_rule_impacts.rationale: Prevent a press-release summary from being treated as the complete official Problem E statement.
Enforce sign, unit, stock-flow, quality, environmental, transfer, and return-flow consistency.
Bound scarcity-indicator semantics and require access, quality, reliability, ecology, space, season, and distribution.
Turn consequential hydrologic and behavioral simplifications into tested scenarios.
Require aligned definitions, years, geographies, units, versions, and observed-versus-projected labels.
Replace algebraically circular indicator checks and narrative plausibility with independent validation.
Force reconciliation of the incompatible 2031 and 2083-2093 forecasts.
Constrain sparse polynomial interpolation and block unsupported extrapolation beyond 2050.
Propagate climate, structural, demand, implementation, and adoption uncertainty into decisions.
Require a complete causal, capacity, cost, timeline, operations, adoption, externality, and feasibility chain for interventions.
Replace national 100% crop substitution based on water depth with a full food-water transition model.
Retain downstream health, gender, livelihood, ecological, and interregional burdens.
Add global and structural robustness and decision-reversal analysis.
Cap precision, prediction, feasibility, and policy language at evidence strength.
Require figures to show the unit, reconciled baseline, full claim horizon, threshold, intervention timing, and uncertainty basis.
Make sign, arithmetic, forecast, intervention, crossing, and figure claims reproducible and regression-tested.

unresolved_questions: Can a complete authoritative 2016 Problem E statement be located outside the current corpus?
What units and data transformation produce forecast curves near EWR 1200 in 2000 when the stated 2009 baseline is 20.75 m3 or 5481.59 gallons per person?
Was the complex EWR sign reversal a typesetting error, and which sign was implemented in MATLAB?
What polyfit degree, scaling, coefficients, source knot values, and upper-lower construction generated each curve?
How are the preliminary negative-before-2031 result, the half-by-2031 summary, and the 2083-2093 zero interval reconciled?
Were watershed curves generated with the reported factor-of-ten arithmetic error or a different code value?
What costs, build rates, utilization, energy, collection, quality, siting, and agricultural delivery assumptions support 651 wastewater plants in three years?
What rice and wheat areas, irrigation shares, effective rainfall, yield, trade, diet, prices, and adoption paths support the millet scenario?
How were zero-crossing intervals beyond 2050 calculated and tested for polynomial extrapolation instability?
